segments.t: Andrea Martel wakes up late in her apartment and discovers that her star client Jose Garcia is missing. When the film crew arrives to pick him up, Andrea runs to check on baby Flora only to find her crib completely empty. Let's listen to her morning panic in French first.
Putain! Quelle heure est-il?
José? Il faut te lever maintenant!
Dépêche-toi, on est en retard.
José, où es-tu passé?
Allô Andréa? Je viens chercher José.
Écoute, je le cherche aussi.
Il n'est pas avec toi?
Non, il n'est plus là!
La production attend sur le plateau.
Je te rappelle tout de suite.
Mon cœur, il faut te réveiller.
On est en retard pour la crèche.
Flora? Où est mon bébé?
Non, ce n'est pas possible!
Let's examine the conversation line by line and explore the French expressions.
Putain! Quelle heure est-il?
'Damn! What time is it?' Andrea realizes that her alarm failed to ring. The swear word 'damn' is very common in informal French to express shock.
José? Il faut te lever maintenant!
'Jose? You have to get up now!' Andrea calls out into the apartment to wake her client. The impersonal expression 'it' expresses necessity.
Dépêche-toi, on est en retard.
'Hurry up, we are late.' Andrea stresses the urgent schedule for the film set. The reflexive imperative 'hurry up' means hurry up.
José, où es-tu passé?
'Jose, where did you go?' Andrea searches through the rooms and finds the couch empty. The interrogative 'where' asks about location.
Allô Andréa? Je viens chercher José.
'Hello Andrea? I am coming to pick up Jose.' The production driver rings the doorbell from the street. The near-future phrase 'come' means coming to pick up.
Écoute, je le cherche aussi.
'Listen, I am looking for him too.' Andrea confesses that her guest has vanished. The direct object pronoun 'him' replaces Jose.
Il n'est pas avec toi?
'He is not with you?' The driver is astonished that the actor is missing. The negative structure 'not' surrounds the verb.
Non, il n'est plus là!
'No, he is no longer here!' Andrea confirms that Jose disappeared without a word. The adverb 'anymore' indicates that he was there before.
La production attend sur le plateau.
'Production is waiting on set.' The driver warns that the filming crew cannot afford delays. The noun 'film set' refers to a film set.
Je te rappelle tout de suite.
'I call you back immediately.' Andrea ends the phone call to investigate the apartment. The idiom 'immediately' means right away.
Mon cœur, il faut te réveiller.
'Sweetheart, you must wake up.' Andrea enters the nursery to get her baby daughter ready. The pet name 'mon coeur' is a loving term of endearment.
On est en retard pour la crèche.
'We are late for the daycare.' Andrea rushes over to the small bed. The feminine noun 'daycare center' designates a daycare center for infants.
Flora? Où est mon bébé?
'Flora? Where is my baby?' Andrea stares at the unoccupied sheets in disbelief. The possessive adjective 'my' agrees with the masculine noun 'baby'.
Non, ce n'est pas possible!

'No, this is not possible!' Andrea panics when she realizes that both Jose and Flora are gone. The demonstrative phrase 'ce n'est pas possible' expresses utter disbelief. Now let's listen to the complete discussion once more to reinforce the vocabulary.

José? Il faut te lever maintenant!

José, où es-tu passé?
Allô Andréa? Je viens chercher José.

Il n'est pas avec toi?
Non, il n'est plus là!
La production attend sur le plateau.
Je te rappelle tout de suite.
Mon cœur, il faut te réveiller.
On est en retard pour la crèche.
Flora? Où est mon bébé?
Non, ce n'est pas possible!

Andrea discovers that both her movie star client and her infant daughter have vanished from the apartment. Terrified that Jose took the baby without permission, she prepares to race across Paris. Now let's listen to the scene one last time.
José est parti avec ma fille!
